Hello Dear Linux users,

I wonder how did you manager to move away from Windows and what was it really that made you a linux only user? I'm a passionate PC gamer and for the most time it's the only reason why i struggle to move away from M$ products.

I know you can dual boot, but that does not seem to be the right solution.

What was your experience moving away from Windows?

I keep a windows box purely for gaming. ( Which also make it devoid of any useful data for Microsoft. )

At first it was because gaming machines are usually pretty noisy ( but through the upgrades it isn't really the case for it anymore ) then I kept it that way so I can wipe the gaming machine if an upgrade need it without worries.
Having a fallback computer when the other is tied to something else is nice too.
i might consider that i will build a new Linux box and then use my old one to only play games on. Sounds pretty good to me.
You'll probably get more bang for your buck to use your new computer for gaming and your old computer with Linux. The sys-reqs for Linux are pretty low.

I'm big into gaming, too. But I was never one to have to get the latest games. I always played what I enjoyed and never bought into the hype. So, when I first started using Linux, I fell in love with it and was pretty easy to switch. I found games on Linux that I could play. And I enjoyed the hell out of those games. Now that 25% of the games on Steam are on Linux, it's just that much better.

The entire PC gaming scene will change within the next five years, is my bet.

The more promotion and support Valve puts into SteamOS/SteamBoxes, the more likely third party developers/publishers will be to release on the platform. The more titles available, the more incentive there will be to improve proprietary driver support for Linux.

I've just recently made the switch, and while it sucks I cannot get every title I want to play on Linux from Steam/GOG etc..., I'll gladly take that trade off in the short to medium term, if it means getting out from under MS.
I use all 3 OS's, but my main reason for getting in to Linux is knowledge, programming and security. I currently run Kali but I need to check out Tails.

I had a good laptop with Win 8. I already disliked that OS with the hamfisted touchscreen UI which was a frustrating waste of space. Win 8.1 was a little better, but still annoying. Once Win 10 came along, I had updates disabled already because I've always found them annoying anyway. Then I started hearing about the shady spying stuff, at the same time, my graphics card seemed to be broken, so I thought that was a good time to switch. I jumped in with both feet and installed Linux Mint Cinnamon 17.2 on my machine. My graphics card that didn't seem to work on windows anymore, worked on linux; the main games I play, Dota 2, CSGO, Insurgency and Starcraft 2 and 100 other games of my 300 on Steam worked. Even the sound quality was improved somehow, I was impressed. Mint felt a lot like win 7. I dual booted for a while, but then switched all my documents + music over to my linux partition, once I realized that I actually liked the OS better and deleted windows. I started learning more about the background of Linux and the whole GNU + FOSS philosophy. I'm now experimenting with an installation of Arch Linux for performance gains and to further my knowledge of the OS. I have also taken up an interest in programming and computer security, I hope to one day be able to contribute to FOSS projects. I think my conversion is complete, I couldn't care less about windows now, I don't need it for anything, I hope that cancer dies.

I'm a big gamer and over time have slowly moved to Linux. It started with trying to only use programs on my windows machine that had a linux version. Once I had pretty much all of my main use cases covered I was able to make the switch. As for gaming I'll admit I've had to sacrifice a bit in order to stay on Linux but I guess my willingness to do that comes from the fact that I strongly believe that it's better to have choice than to be restricted to windows if you want to game on PC. The only way gaming will be able to escape from the windows stranglehold is if people move and refuse to buy windows-only games. It sucks to be among the first to do so, but I believe someone has to do it so here I am. In the meantime the gaming situation over here isn't really even all that bad: CSGO, Left4Dead2, Albion Online, Ark Survival Evolved, Rust, TF2 and tons of indie games are things that have been greatly enjoyed by me. There's plenty of great games to play and while you may not be able to play some of the AAA stuff that's being released by certain studios, if you can't find something fun to play that runs natively then you're a picky gamer indeed.

I also get some benefits for my sacrifice however. Deeper control, every time I run into a problem and fix it myself I improve my understanding and knowledge of my OS. After only a few years I'm way more comfortable on linux than I ever was on Windows. Windows problems never seemed logical and the fixes always seemed janky most of the time. Like duct taping a machine that's already held together with more duct tape and paper clips, even if it works it doesn't feel right and you're afraid to go poking around to try and improve the situation because something else would inevitably fall apart if you did. Fixing Linux is different, it's like opening up a Ferrari because you heard a sound that sounded like a loose nozzle. Then of course finding a loose valve or nozzle, tightening that shit up while also noticing that one of the other valves was in a sub-optimal position, so you fixed that too. Then starting the car to hear that everything runs perfectly once again maybe better than before. Most of the time Linux problems are logical and the fix is logical because nothing is really hidden from you.

I don't know about the privacy stuff because I don't really know how bad windows 10 is but all the negative hype on the net is not making me want to find out, despite the fact that it's probably blown way out of proportion. I don't know about security either, I do know that on windows I had to have anti-virus stuff running constantly and had some issues with adware that wouldn't let itself be shut down but on Linux have never had such problems so far. Possibly only because the baddies are targeting windows and macs as the more used platforms. But for now I'm really happy with my machine running fast and reliably without all that other shit.

Steam runs well over here assuming you're on a distro relatively close to ubuntu or debian. I haven't really had any trouble with individual games not working. A few of them can't seem to figure out my multimonitor set up but I always find a workaround to make them behave the way I want that I can live with. I feel like these things are issues that will be sorted out with time as developers get more experience developing for linux.
I use W7 for gaming and a Linux Mint pc for every day use, was very easy since I've been around Computer's a long time starting with an Altair 8800 kit.

I dual boot but I very rarely touch my Windows 7 partition, even if I have to bust my ass to get games working on the others. It's mainly just disgust that keeps me off Windows but that disgust is something that happens gradually after using something way better.

The adjustment period is the main factor in deciding if you stick with it. When you first switch, you'll gripe that things aren't how they are in Windows. There's features that didn't come with your distro or desktop and you yearn for them. You start looking up alternatives and slowly you make it more like what you're used to. Then you start playing with things that Windows can't do. You start thinking "how did I ever live without a {package manager|tiling WM|multiple workspaces|full-featured shell}?" You certainly don't miss installers that try to sneak adware into your computer, dealing with a registry, untrustworthy proprietary software to fix a small problem, the incredible amount of bloat, or having to install drivers for fucking everything under the sun (and then Microsoft's automatic installer overwriting them anyway). You'll be amazed that software developed by tens of thousands of volunteers working toward a unified design standard meshes together better than something designed by a single company.

So you boot back into your Windows partition to play a game. Your first thought is "why do I bother?"

Your best option is some form of hardware pass though. Not every Intel and AMD CPU and motherboard supports it but you need VT-d support if you have an Intel build or AMD-V if, well its kinda obvious.

Hardware pass though allows you to do a neat little thing like pass direct access of your hardware though to a virtual machine allowing you to have a virtualized copy of Windows with full access to your graphics card. It sounds great in theory and it does work really really well if everything is properly configured.

Its not an easy couple clicks and you're done kind of thing, if youve got the right hardware and plenty of time on your hands it could be the perfect answer to your problem. https://teksyndicate.com/videos/gta-v-linux-skylake-build-hardware-vm-passthrough

I'd had little to no knowledge of how computers work when I switched to Linux. It was definitely a learning experience, but as I learned, the easier it became and the more satisfied I was with my new OS. I still use a Windows partition for games that don't work well on Linux.
If you name an application, I'll be happy to recommend some similar ones. I've used a lot of FOSS software.
